aliases.name: IRIDIUM
aliases.vendor: Microsoft (2022 post says DEV-0665 was 'previously tracked' under this name; current mapping assigns IRIDIUM to Seashell Blizzard, so conflicting)

identification.summary: Sunglow Blizzard is the current Microsoft name listed for the former designation DEV-0665 in Microsoft's public threat actor naming mapping [S4]. DEV-0665 was the Microsoft cluster associated with the destructive FoxBlade (HermeticWiper) attacks on Ukraine that began on 2022-02-23 [S1]. The mapping gives no origin or description for the entry [S4].
identification.firstObserved: 2022-02-23 (FoxBlade/HermeticWiper destructive attack first discovered, per Microsoft) [S1]
identification.notes: NAMING CONFLICT. Microsoft's February 2022 post says FoxBlade events were attributed with medium confidence to 'IRIDIUM (previously tracked as DEV-0665)' [S1]. The current mapping file instead lists DEV-0665 as an alias of Sunglow Blizzard and lists IRIDIUM as an alias of Seashell Blizzard (with Sandworm, APT44, VOODOO BEAR and others) [S4]. The two sources do not agree on whether DEV-0665 belongs to Sunglow Blizzard or to the IRIDIUM/Seashell Blizzard cluster, so no facts from the Seashell Blizzard cluster are merged into this record. Microsoft tracks the separate January 2022 WhisperGate actor as DEV-0586 [S1]. Microsoft calls IsaacWiper 'Lasainraw' and says it had not linked it to an attributed actor [S1].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributed FoxBlade-associated events with medium confidence to the cluster it then named IRIDIUM (previously DEV-0665) [S1]. ESET stated it had found no tangible connection to a known threat actor and no significant code similarity to other samples in its collection [S2]. No source gathered attributes the Sunglow Blizzard name to a state sponsor.
attribution.basis: Microsoft MSTIC assessment in its February 2022 Ukraine post [S1]. The mapping file gives no origin for Sunglow Blizzard [S4].

objectives: Microsoft assessed a continued risk of destructive activity from the group based on follow-on intrusions observed since 2022-02-23 [S1].

targeting.notes: Microsoft describes the FoxBlade attack as affecting hundreds of systems across government, IT, financial and energy organizations, mainly in or linked to Ukraine [S1]. ESET observed HermeticWiper on hundreds of systems in at least five Ukrainian organizations [S2]. Whether these victims are all attributable to Sunglow Blizzard specifically is not established given the naming conflict.

capabilities.summary: Microsoft's FoxBlade is the same family as ESET's HermeticWiper and HermeticWizard, with SonicVote corresponding to HermeticRansom [S1]. ESET describes HermeticWiper as the wiper, HermeticWizard as a worm that spreads over local networks via WMI and SMB, and HermeticRansom as Go-based ransomware acting as a decoy [S2]. The malware was signed with a certificate issued to Hermetica Digital Ltd, which DigiCert revoked on 2022-02-24 at ESET's request [S2]. Microsoft notes use of a renamed SysInternals sdelete (cdel.exe) for targeted secure deletion in the associated cluster [S1].

campaigns.name: FoxBlade / HermeticWiper attacks on Ukraine
campaigns.summary: Destructive malware discovered on 2022-02-23 affecting hundreds of systems, mainly in or linked to Ukraine, hours before the 2022-02-24 invasion; Microsoft attributed associated events with medium confidence to DEV-0665 (then named IRIDIUM) and warned of follow-on intrusions [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: IsaacWiper (Lasainraw) activity
campaigns.summary: ESET reported a second wiper, IsaacWiper, against a Ukrainian government network; Microsoft calls it Lasainraw and had not linked it to an attributed actor, so it is not assigned to Sunglow Blizzard [S1][S2].

diamond.adversary: Microsoft cluster DEV-0665, now listed as Sunglow Blizzard; sponsor not stated in gathered sources [S4].
diamond.capability: FoxBlade/HermeticWiper, HermeticWizard worm (WMI/SMB), HermeticRansom decoy, renamed sdelete [S1][S2].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian government, IT, financial and energy organizations [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Destructive activity timed hours before the 2022-02-24 invasion of Ukraine [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and domain networks reachable by SMB/WMI lateral movement [S2].

gaps: Microsoft's 2022 post names IRIDIUM (previously DEV-0665) while the current mapping lists DEV-0665 under Sunglow Blizzard and IRIDIUM under Seashell Blizzard [S1][S4]. The reason for the divergence (rename, split or correction) was not found in gathered sources.

No state sponsor is stated for Sunglow Blizzard in gathered sources; the mapping file leaves origin blank [S4]. Other vendors' views on HermeticWiper attribution (for example Recorded Future, Virus Bulletin slides) were seen only as search snippets and are not cited.
Initial access, dwell time and C2 infrastructure for the HermeticWiper intrusions were not obtained.
No activity attributed to Sunglow Blizzard after 2022 was found.

Primary documents not opened: ESET original blog (host unreachable by fetch, content taken from search summary), CISA AR22-115B, Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2022 chapter, MISP galaxy and Malpedia entries.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Windows domain networks of government, IT, financial and energy organizations are key terrain; wipers target availability of endpoints [S1][S2]. STEP 2: The actor-cluster pattern shows destructive payloads staged and executed within hours of a kinetic escalation [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Observed template is a signed wiper plus a worm for SMB/WMI spread and a decoy ransomware [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is destructive wiper attacks against a state's government and critical-sector networks timed to kinetic or political escalation. MDCOA is the same worm-enabled spread across a coalition partner's networks whose boundary is shared with the target state [S2]. Candidate indicators: renamed sdelete use against C:, newly signed binaries from unfamiliar publishers, and anomalous WMI/SMB lateral movement [S1][S2]. Attribution of this cluster is unresolved (see gaps).
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor naming changes, since DEV-0665 maps differently across Microsoft sources [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: destructive response on partner networks requires coordination with the host nation and supported command; this record gives no authority guidance. (3) Mission assurance: validated offline backups, tamper protection and current endpoint detections are the Microsoft-recommended mitigations [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators and certificate-revocation requests with industry and partners, as ESET did with DigiCert [S2].
